L2 collateral, local stablecoin issuance and the Curve network
30 September 2026. This study evaluates an issuer-mediated route from asserted pARB assets to
existing PulseChain stablecoins. It examines every pool returned by eight selected responsive Curve
registry sources, and audits the principal local issuer branches. It does not certify all possible pARB
deployments, every stablecoin's operational mint path, or common human control of their authorities.
Finding and scope
The proposed route is technically meaningful: an authorized source position can become collateral for a
destination issuer, which can mint the existing local token address recognized by an existing Curve
pool. A newly bridged representation need not become a Curve coin. Most of the proposed governance
work consequently concerns the issuer, its collateral, valuation and mint permissions.
Reserve's collateral-plugin architecture is especially suitable. Origin requires compatible supported-asset
accounting. The current mUSD implementation appears to need an upgrade for a genuinely new
collateral address. Some other tokens offer an even shorter authorized-mint branch. None of those
architectural observations proves who controls the necessary authority or that source collateral is
currently available.
The hypothesis that every Curve stablecoin's governance was acquired is stronger than the mechanism
needs. A useful subset can connect several major pools. Literal universal governance control also
conflicts with immutable issuer designs such as Liquity V1. Such coins may still be bought, traded, or
minted through their existing permitted collateral route.

All chain operations were getters, view quotes, code or storage reads. No signing, broadcasts,
administrative changes, privileged impersonation, storage overrides or state-changing simulations were
performed. Positive mintability cannot be established solely by configuration getters or a quote that
omits transfers and permissions.
The maintained paper (main paper) presents the mechanism simply. This study supplies the distinctions
needed to assess it.

The two source branches and the destination conversion
The first branch matches the proposal to mint OUSD, eUSD, mUSD or other stables on L2 from source
stable inputs, bridge them, and use their representations to obtain L1 issuance. The second uses
lending, vault or LP receipts directly. Neither branch presupposes that a historical Ethereum issuer was
deployed natively on historical Arbitrum. Custom pARB deployments are possible assumptions, but need
an RPC, chain identity and contract list before their actual state can be inspected.
“e-stables” is retained as a description of source inputs. It has not been assigned a particular Reserve
eUSD address, an Ethereum dollar entitlement or a backing model. Those identities materially affect
valuation and redeemability.

An L2 OUSD representation does not become local Origin OUSD because the names match. An ordinary
canonical withdrawal can release existing L1 escrow, while a custom representation can create a
different collateral token. A destination issuer can then convert that new collateral into its own canonical
output if its rules allow it.
There is no general requirement to create a new LP before that conversion. An issuer normally receives
collateral through its own deposit/mint path. An LP receipt is useful only if that receipt itself is accepted
collateral or a permitted strategy position. “Pair it inside the protocol” must specify whether this means a
vault deposit, basket membership, a strategy holding, a collateralized loan, or an LP position.
The simplest path before governance changes
First ask whether the bridge can deliver an already accepted local collateral address. If it can
deliver local DAI, USDC, USDT or a required lending receipt, the corresponding issuer can use its existing
rules. There is no need to whitelist a foreign stablecoin merely to mint a local one.
That shortcut may use escrow or relayer cash. It does not establish a limitless supply of local collateral. A
bridge withdrawal is bounded by its backing model; a liquidity fill is bounded by spendable inventory and
settlement. The benefit is avoiding collateral onboarding and preserving existing issuer accounting.
Next ask whether the destination token already has a controlled authorized minter. DOLA's verified token
allows its operator or approved minters to create supply. XAI's verified token permits its owner to mint.
alUSD uses administrative whitelist and ceiling controls. FRAX uses authorized pools. If the coordinated-
control assumption includes those exact powers, some branches can issue their local Curve coin without
first bridging a new receipt.
This is stronger support for a multi-issuer supply thesis, but does not mean all token owners can mint all
assets. Source code must establish the role's powers; live reads must identify its holder; contract holders
require their own execution path; any ceiling, timelock, pause, collateral or liquidity constraint must be
carried forward.

The current asset list contains exactly local DAI, USDT and USDC. Capital operations are unpaused. The
mint predicate requires a supported asset, positive deposit, acceptable oracle price and minimum
output. The valuation is capped at 1e8, and the minimum acceptable oracle price is 99,800,000. These
are contract accounting units, not a test of dollar redeemability. At the pinned block the three sampled
oracle prices pass that threshold.
The code mints OUSD and transfers the deposited collateral within one atomic transaction. A failed later
transfer or strategy action reverts the transaction. It may rebase and allocate strategies during minting;
passing the sampled price predicate is not proof those downstream actions succeed.
For a new L2 receipt, the technical issues are:
Exact support of its destination address and usable pricing.
Decimal normalization and whether value is represented by a growing balance or a growing share
price.
Rebase, strategy allocation, redemption and total-value accounting compatibility.
A bridge redemption rule and source withdrawal route that can support the receipt's stated value.
A non-rebasing share worth 1.20 underlying units would still encounter the core's $1 mint-price ceiling
per normalized token. Correct treatment may need a compatible wrapper, strategy or accounting
upgrade. A price below $0.998 prevents ordinary issuance even if the asset has been added.
The vault governor and token governor are 0x35918cde7233f2dd33fa41ae3cb6ae0e42e0e69f. Its verified Timelock
source checks proposer and executor roles; the sampled minimum delay is 172,800 seconds, two
days. The vault delegates administrative calls to 0x1ef0553feb80e6f133cae3092e38f0b23da6452b. That address
and the current oracle lack verified source in this explorer sample. The core exposes a governor-only way
to replace its admin implementation. Ordinary asset-onboarding behavior of the present admin is
therefore unresolved, rather than assumed from modern Origin documentation.
No complete proposer-holder/voting-control census was established here. Activity at an OGV staking
proxy is evidence of activity, not proof of proposal authority or common ownership. Modern Origin
contracts describe current upstream development; they are not substituted for the sampled older multi-
asset implementation.
The existing destination is OUSD/3CRV at 0x87650d7bbfc3a9f10587d7778206671719d9910d. Successful issuance of
that exact OUSD token does not require a new pool coin. Directly sending a different bridged OUSD
representation does not provide the same path.

A new collateral route generally requires plugin registration, prime-basket selection, activation/refresh of
the reference basket and passage of the issuance checks. Merely registering a plugin does not make a
deposit issue eUSD. The existing v2 core can support a suitable plugin without necessarily replacing the
core implementation.
A single-asset basket is an architectural possibility if governance configures a valid compatible collateral
asset. A partial basket allocation requires all remaining components. If 100 target-value units provide
one 25% component, issuance of 400 units requires 300 target-value units in the other components as
well. It is not fourfold unbacked purchasing power.
Issuance refreshes collateral, requires a sound basket, observes throttles, obtains a rounded-up deposit
quote and transfers every required collateral token into BackingManager. The sampled cached basket
status is SOUND, fullyCollateralized is true, and Main is unpaused/unfrozen. Older saved plugin reads
nevertheless returned unusable price ranges and stale May 2023 feeds. Cached status is not proof that
the next refreshing issuance passes. Mutating refresh or issue calls were not simulated.

Each input at 10 million whole units reverts on weight limits. Local OUSD and Reserve eUSD at both
tested sizes revert as invalid assets. These tests establish the quote branch's behavior. They do not
execute a collateral transfer, run mint's full healthy/permission path or prove backing/liquidity.
The verified source includes a library helper that can add a basket asset. The current token
implementation does not expose it through an ordinary public collateral-addition function. It exposes
minting, weight-limit adjustment, integration migration and other administration. The presence of a
helper in a source bundle is not a callable onboarding interface.
Consequently, accepted underlying delivered by the bridge is the simpler route. Accepting an entirely
new bridged receipt appears to need a compatible upgrade or a separately constructed route that ends
in an existing accepted asset. An integration migration alters where an existing basket asset is invested;
it is not an authorization to treat a different ERC20 as that basket asset.

Fraxlend's primary description distinguishes lending shares from borrowing. Compound III distinguishes
interest-bearing base supply from non-interest-bearing collateral. Radiant rT okens, Beefy vaults, Stargate
liquidity claims and Pendle's principal/yield distinction supply the architecture references. Camelot V2
and Uniswap V3 require different position handling.
GMX is particularly time-sensitive: its current archived V1 documentation says upstream GLP minting has
been phased out. Historical GLP capability must not be presented as a currently usable upstream
product or an automatically operating pARB deployment. Similar version/date checks apply to new
Yearn, Silo, Alchemix and stablecoin products.
Silo's classic interface distinguishes collateral shares, collateral-only shares and debt shares. It uses the
term “bridge assets” for assets connecting isolated lending markets. That terminology does not prove
cross-chain transport. XAI token issuance and a Silo's borrowing/liquidity constraints must be tested as
separate layers.
Every row can potentially supply a representation for an L1 issuer after suitable integration. None gives
a generic right to deposit its receipt into unchanged Origin, Reserve or mStable. The most
direct candidates are transferable stable lending or vault receipts with understandable withdrawal rights.
NFT positions, mixed-risk LPs, leveraged vaults and expiring claims require more adaptation and
valuation.

The 382 unique direct/underlying token addresses include 98 dollar-stable label candidates and 32

There are 176 direct-coin 3CRV pools and 64 direct-coin FRAXBP pools. Other stable pools include
direct currency pairs, alternative multi-coin bases, lending pools, non-dollar pairs, mixed crypto/stable
pools and nested LP positions. Not every Curve pool contains a stablecoin or belongs to the pDAI peg
network.
The full census is available as pool CSV, pool JSON and token inventory. The CSV includes coin identities,
underlying identities, registry source, hub classification and raw per-coin balance results. Unknown reads
remain unknown. Raw quantities lack decimal normalization and executable-price meaning.
Each pool must be assessed under the same distinctions:
Same existing local coin: successful issuance can feed ordinary swaps/liquidity without replacing
pool coins.
Different bridged token: current coin membership provides no direct route unless an existing
conversion exists.
Base-pool or receipt coin: the backing inventory and withdrawal route must be traced recursively.
Empty or incomplete balances: registration is not an executable trade or funded exit.
Mixed/non-dollar assets: quotes, risk and FX differ from the dollar-stable model.
Corrected balance getters show 350 pools with at least one nonzero coin balance, 235 with every
returned coin balance zero, and 34 with incomplete balance reads. Among direct-coin 3CRV pools these
counts are 67, 89 and 20; among FRAXBP pools they are 37, 27 and zero. Nonzero inventory is not a
successful trade quote or a dollar valuation.

authority getters, source-verification status where fetched, and unresolved effective control/collateral
acceptance. This covers candidates without pretending every symbol is an audited issuer. Unrecognized
symbols and remaining token addresses stay in the full token/pool catalogue.
The census preserves all cases. It does not attest that all listed pools are active, liquid, source-audited,
permissionless or correctly valued. A source audit and trade-size view quote remain necessary before
claiming an individual route is currently executable. Older named-pool transaction evidence remains in
the Curve history study (Appendix 8).
Bridges, delays and the multi-year financing idea
Five bridge families remain relevant: ordinary escrow withdrawals, specialized/custom gateways, source-
native burn/destination mint systems, Portal receipt financing, and liquidity-fill bridges such as Across.
They provide different inventory, token identities, delays and liabilities.
An ordinary Arbitrum gateway can release an existing local token from escrow. It does not automatically
mint extra canonical supply. A new collateral representation requires its own authorized mapping/minter
or a compatible bridge implementation. The bridge inventory (Appendix 4) preserves 129 registered
router mappings plus seven examined extra candidates. Its escrow findings do not refute a separately
authorized issuer accepting new bridged collateral.

Across can accelerate supported transfers through liquidity fills, subject to the copied/custom system's
routes, relayers, repayment and dispute conditions. Controlling a governance role does not by itself
place arbitrary stablecoin or receipt support into its current token/route mappings. A fill delivering
canonical local USDC is one branch; minting a new collateral representation is another. The Across
authority study (Appendix 3) separates those checks.
The saved copied pARB Rollup confirmation getter returns 45,818 L1 blocks. This is a block count, not
a fixed multi-year settlement date; accepted ancestry, admission, challenges and chain progress affect
confirmation. The saved Across Hub liveness getter returns 7,200 seconds, two hours. That bundle
period does not equal a user fill's latency, final reimbursement time or a Portal maturity. Both
observations and their raw responses are retained in the deferred campaign study (Appendix 34).
Delay must be stated per route. It includes source issuance, any collateral withdrawal queue or maturity,
bridge confirmation/finality, governance installation, issuer throttles/basket warm-up, market
accumulation, and eventual debt/backing settlement. Origin's two-day timelock and the reported
mStable seven-day upgrade delay are configuration clocks. Reserve's voting clocks are block-based and
its sampled timelock is three days. These are not a common bridge waiting period.
For the proposed ten-second campaign, 50bn input units at 10,000 per slot require approximately 579
uninterrupted days. A 1,000-unit allocation extends it to roughly 15.9 years. A pause while pDAI meets
the target extends calendar time. Pool replenishment and third-party demand determine whether spaced
orders improve overall acquisition; cadence does not create purchasing power or erase aggregate
slippage.
A lending/vault receipt can remain invested for years if its actual rules permit it. The earlier Portal source
review found aggregate unbacked accounting without a per-mint settlement countdown. Current positive
Portal issuance is nevertheless blocked by all 17 observed unbacked caps being zero. New permissions,
usable supply caps and authorized bridge execution are prerequisites. Multiple bridges share headroom;
later issuance does not erase earlier unbacked amounts.
The complete examined 86ff V3 debt inventory includes twelve nonzero assets. Separate matching
receipts can retire its account debts if legitimate account execution is available, but those burned
receipts cannot also fund purchases. Portal exposure persists after receipt-based borrower repayment.
Debt reduction does not transfer ownership of the borrower's remaining collateral. The deferred
campaign study (Appendix 34) retains exact amounts, rates, time scenarios and source predicates.
Economic merits and the limits of the deterministic claim
The strongest version of the thesis is a coordinated collateral-and-issuance network. It can create
market-facing local coins, spread acquisition over different pools, retain yield-producing source collateral
and accumulate ownership of pStables and their liquidity. It may use existing issuer coin addresses,
avoid changes to established pool contracts and give a local unit multiple conversion paths. Direct mint
authorities could simplify selected branches further.
The mechanism needs a consolidated balance sheet. If a source position is deposited as backing for local
eUSD, the operator cannot simultaneously count that position as free settlement inventory. If eUSD then
backs another issued coin, the second issuance creates another claim along the chain, rather than
independent unencumbered capital. Genuine fee or interest income can grow net resources; a controlled
borrower paying a controlled lender shifts funds within the group. Repeated controlled swaps also incur
costs rather than generating outside fee income.
Issuer outputs enter Curve against finite opposing inventory. A metacoin swap buys existing pStables
and can move their relative prices; a liquidity deposit supplies inventory and mints an LP claim. An
unbalanced deposit may leave the pool more unbalanced. “Rebalancing” should mean a defined
improvement in a specified balance, not every addition of a minted token.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 272

A network valuation may recognize 100 source units as 100 target units, or apply a haircut/LTV that
permits less issuance. An oracle can assign $1 to an asserted source asset. That creates a contract-
accounting value; redeemable dollars or freely saleable collateral require additional evidence. Discount,
liquidity, bridge loss, withdrawal queues and liquidation thresholds can constrain what the issuer's
liabilities actually buy.
Ownership concentration improves the operator's ability to supply liquidity and manage circulating float.
Acquiring every outside pDAI removes outside pDAI sellers at that moment. Issuing or selling tokens
again recreates outside claims. A funded redemption venue can implement a definite exchange rule
within its available inventory and permissions. A V2 LP's reserve ratio changes with trades, even when
one entity owns the LP . A controlled network can intervene, but a universal price guarantee needs a
specified payment asset and funded intervention capacity.
Internal parity among pDAI and locally managed stables is a useful target. Calling it a dollar peg requires
an external dollar reference or a defined dollar-deliverable claim. An ETH/WBTC exit can supply market
convertibility without fixing dollar proceeds. Frozen copied oracles and a hypothetical fixed GHO
accounting price cannot replace that exit inventory. The managed-peg study (Appendix 45) and portal
pricing study (Appendix 48) preserve the earlier accounting/market distinction.
The network may still be powerful under the coordinated-control assumption. The appropriate
conditional statement is specific: the system can issue through compatible authorized branches, acquire
assets at executable quotes, and support a defined conversion within funded capacity. The evidence
does not yet establish every source deployment, every controller's effective execution, universal issuer
control, an installed cross-chain collateral basket, or unlimited external redemption.

collateral-20260930

for example:

pulsechain_issuer_route_predicates_corrected_20260930.json --output artifacts/pulsechain-issuer-collateral-
replay/route-predicates.json
Do not use the probe's default mode: earlier default operations include state-changing simulations
outside this task's scope. Every manifest used here has been checked to contain only getters/view calls
or read RPC methods. Decimal quantities must be JSON integers; hex strings must start with 0x.

now rejects malformed string arguments. In particular, early zero-quantity quote reverts are not issuer
evidence. The retained evidence note identifies these exclusions.

L2 collateral, local stablecoin issuance and the Curve network
30 September 2026. This study evaluates an issuer-mediated route from asserted pARB assets to
existing PulseChain stablecoins. It examines every pool returned by eight selected responsive Curve
registry sources, and audits the principal local issuer branches. It does not certify all possible pARB
deployments, every stablecoin's operational mint path, or common human control of their authorities.
Finding and scope
The proposed route is technically meaningful: an authorized source position can become collateral for a
destination issuer, which can mint the existing local token address recognized by an existing Curve
pool. A newly bridged representation need not become a Curve coin. Most of the proposed governance
work consequently concerns the issuer, its collateral, valuation and mint permissions.
Reserve's collateral-plugin architecture is especially suitable. Origin requires compatible supported-asset
accounting. The current mUSD implementation appears to need an upgrade for a genuinely new
collateral address. Some other tokens offer an even shorter authorized-mint branch. None of those
architectural observations proves who controls the necessary authority or that source collateral is
currently available.
The hypothesis that every Curve stablecoin's governance was acquired is stronger than the mechanism
needs. A useful subset can connect several major pools. Literal universal governance control also
conflicts with immutable issuer designs such as Liquity V1. Such coins may still be bought, traded, or
minted through their existing permitted collateral route.

deployed natively on historical Arbitrum. Custom pARB deployments are possible assumptions, but need
an RPC, chain identity and contract list before their actual state can be inspected.

An L2 OUSD representation does not become local Origin OUSD because the names match. An ordinary
canonical withdrawal can release existing L1 escrow, while a custom representation can create a
different collateral token. A destination issuer can then convert that new collateral into its own canonical
output if its rules allow it.
There is no general requirement to create a new LP before that conversion. An issuer normally receives
collateral through its own deposit/mint path. An LP receipt is useful only if that receipt itself is accepted
collateral or a permitted strategy position. “Pair it inside the protocol” must specify whether this means a
vault deposit, basket membership, a strategy holding, a collateralized loan, or an LP position.
The simplest path before governance changes
First ask whether the bridge can deliver an already accepted local collateral address. If it can
deliver local DAI, USDC, USDT or a required lending receipt, the corresponding issuer can use its existing
rules. There is no need to whitelist a foreign stablecoin merely to mint a local one.
That shortcut may use escrow or relayer cash. It does not establish a limitless supply of local collateral. A
bridge withdrawal is bounded by its backing model; a liquidity fill is bounded by spendable inventory and
settlement. The benefit is avoiding collateral onboarding and preserving existing issuer accounting.
Next ask whether the destination token already has a controlled authorized minter. DOLA's verified token
allows its operator or approved minters to create supply. XAI's verified token permits its owner to mint.
alUSD uses administrative whitelist and ceiling controls. FRAX uses authorized pools. If the coordinated-
control assumption includes those exact powers, some branches can issue their local Curve coin without
first bridging a new receipt.
This is stronger support for a multi-issuer supply thesis, but does not mean all token owners can mint all
assets. Source code must establish the role's powers; live reads must identify its holder; contract holders
require their own execution path; any ceiling, timelock, pause, collateral or liquidity constraint must be
carried forward.

Economic merits and the limits of the deterministic claim
The strongest version of the thesis is a coordinated collateral-and-issuance network. It can create
market-facing local coins, spread acquisition over different pools, retain yield-producing source collateral
and accumulate ownership of pStables and their liquidity. It may use existing issuer coin addresses,
avoid changes to established pool contracts and give a local unit multiple conversion paths. Direct mint
authorities could simplify selected branches further.
The mechanism needs a consolidated balance sheet. If a source position is deposited as backing for local
eUSD, the operator cannot simultaneously count that position as free settlement inventory. If eUSD then
backs another issued coin, the second issuance creates another claim along the chain, rather than
independent unencumbered capital. Genuine fee or interest income can grow net resources; a controlled
borrower paying a controlled lender shifts funds within the group. Repeated controlled swaps also incur
costs rather than generating outside fee income.
Issuer outputs enter Curve against finite opposing inventory. A metacoin swap buys existing pStables
and can move their relative prices; a liquidity deposit supplies inventory and mints an LP claim. An
unbalanced deposit may leave the pool more unbalanced. “Rebalancing” should mean a defined
improvement in a specified balance, not every addition of a minted token.

A network valuation may recognize 100 source units as 100 target units, or apply a haircut/LTV that

Ownership concentration improves the operator's ability to supply liquidity and manage circulating float.
Acquiring every outside pDAI removes outside pDAI sellers at that moment. Issuing or selling tokens
again recreates outside claims. A funded redemption venue can implement a definite exchange rule
within its available inventory and permissions. A V2 LP's reserve ratio changes with trades, even when
one entity owns the LP . A controlled network can intervene, but a universal price guarantee needs a
specified payment asset and funded intervention capacity.
Internal parity among pDAI and locally managed stables is a useful target. Calling it a dollar peg requires
an external dollar reference or a defined dollar-deliverable claim. An ETH/WBTC exit can supply market
convertibility without fixing dollar proceeds. Frozen copied oracles and a hypothetical fixed GHO
accounting price cannot replace that exit inventory. The managed-peg study (Appendix 45) and portal
pricing study (Appendix 48) preserve the earlier accounting/market distinction.
The network may still be powerful under the coordinated-control assumption. The appropriate
conditional statement is specific: the system can issue through compatible authorized branches, acquire
assets at executable quotes, and support a defined conversion within funded capacity. The evidence
does not yet establish every source deployment, every controller's effective execution, universal issuer
control, an installed cross-chain collateral basket, or unlimited external redemption.
